On Sunday, January 1, 2017 at 1:56:30 PM UTC-5, Jon Fawcett wrote:
> The model seems to do precisely what I need, and it converges much better than before. My particular application is a little different in that I am only trying to predict the probit-transformed mean of each variable (rather than estimate the influence of predictors), but I believe this to be a simple change: I made mu into a parameter representing the mean prevalence for each disorder rather than calculating it on the basis of beta * x[n].

That's fine

> The only other wrinkle is the inclusion of missing data. There are several patients for which we have no measurements for a number of the disorders (this comprises around 12% of the total data we have on hand with the precise disorders affected varying). My understanding based on the earlier incarnation of this model is that for those trials, an unbounded value is imputed instead. As such, I changed y to range from -1 to 1 and coded the missing data as -1 (0’s and 1’s still mean the same; I actually did not think to check until just now, but if Stan could handle the values being NA I may try to keep them as such rather than artificially coding missing values as -1).

The Stan language doesn't have a NA concept so you have to code the missing values as a magic number or pass the nonmissing values in as a giant one-dimensional array and pass in another two-dimensional array indicating where the observed values occur.

> I then extended the if-else statement that sorted and appropriately bounded the data in your code to deal with 0’s and 1’s as before, but with an additional statement dealing with the -1’s as follows:
>
> else {
>    z[d] = inv_Phi(u[n,d]);
> }
>
> This statement ignores the bound variable. In simulations this *seems* to work, but given that I am still learning about the current implementation, I thought I had better check with one of the Oracles.

That should be fine since there are no informative bounds on the t when the outcome is missing.

Ben

I have a (mixture) model with a few latent Gaussian processes, and as you might expect, instantiation is a pain. I generated a toy dataset, and if I the initial parameters to the ground truth of what they should be, sampling still works (though it's pretty darn slow) but I'm not confident (even after running for 5K warmup iterations) I've converged to the stationary distribution. I'd like to check this using a MAP estimate or variational Bayes with ADVI, and neither work.

Here is the output when I run the optimization method (in PyStan):

(env) ➜  src git:(master) python3 dhmm.py --likelihood gaussian --data ../data/toy_x.csv \

 --input ../data/toy_t.csv --test-input ../data/toy_test_t.csv --init ../data/toy_init.pkl \

I think this is weird since presumably the NUTS sampler uses gradient information as well, so I should have (but didn't) seen this when I sampled instead of optmized.

Similarly, with ADVI, I have this different issue (and it says it _can_ evaluate the gradient):

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Add thinning interval to monitor()?
messages.body_plain:
I assume a package would just literally thin then calculate
everything based on the thinned sample.

If you need to save space, thin before you save the draws (as
an argument to the Stan call in whatever interface you're using).
Otherwise, the space all gets allocated anyway, and thinning
afterward just loses information as Ben and Michael were saying.

CmdStan's a bit different --- it streams the draws out to a file.
But again, you can thin before you stream to save space.

- Bob

> On Dec 31, 2016, at 6:17 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Correct.  coda may be trying to do something wacky, but I have no idea what they would be doing.
>
> On Dec 31, 2016, at 6:07 PM, Qian Zhang <qian.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> OK, I think you're saying that there is no need to add a thinning argument to monitor() because thinning cannot be corrected for in the calculation of ESS or Rstat, so I should use the existing monitor() on the thinned samples from the non-STAN software. I'll just do that then.
>>
>> On Saturday, December 31, 2016 at 4:58:16 PM UTC-6, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> Also, what exactly do you expect a thinning argument to the Rhat and
>> ESS calculations would do?  As you lose all of the information you thinned
>> there is no correction for that loss — the best you can do is compute Rhat
>> and ESS using all of the samples that you kept.
>>
>> Note also that Stan uses a more robust calculation for Rhat and ESS that
>> splits each chain, so even without thinning the results from Stan and coda
>> will not in general be the same.  Empirically the coda results tend to miss
>> many of the pathologies that the Stan results catch.
>>
>> On Dec 31, 2016, at 5:50 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>>> On Saturday, December 31, 2016 at 5:42:48 PM UTC-5, Qian Zhang wrote:
>>> Thanks.
>>>
>>> I realize that thinning reduces the effective sample size, but I have to cope with someone else's software, which thins by default. Also thinning could be necessary if you don't have space to store all samples.
>>>
>>> If storeage is a problem, you can thin the chains by specifying the thin argument to sample() or stan(). But thinning after you have already stored them is just sacrificing information for no gain.
>>>
>>> The fact that other software thins by default and Stan doesn't already tells you a lot about the respective dependence among adjacent draws. If NUTS is going well and you were to thin to every fifth draw, the retained draws will be indistinguishable from independent. But your effective sample size would be about half as much as it would be if you didn't thin.

messages.subject: rstan does not find StanHeaders' libraries on multiple architectures (linux) installations
messages.subject_clean: rstan does not find StanHeaders' libraries on multiple architectures (linux) installations
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Presumably, this should/could have been reported much earlier, but I must admit that the last months I had no need to compile a Stan program on my machine.  I was using mostly another machine which has a binary distribution of R installed.  But that machine is currently down and so I had to use my own machine on which R is installed from source, both as a 32-bit architecture and a 64-bit architecture.

To my surprise, compilation failed.  The error message was, essentially:

   /usr/bin/ld: cannot find -lStanHeaders
   collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status

So I thought the problem might be related to Dieter Menne's "Error installing 2.13 on Windows" report, but perhaps not.

My machine is:

    berwin@ECM-DTC-716:~$ uname -a
    Linux ECM-DTC-716 4.4.0-57-generic #78-Ubuntu SMP Fri Dec 9 23:50:32 UTC 2016 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux

And I received the above error message with R 3.3.2, rstan 2.14.1 and StanHeaders 2.14.0 as well with R 3.3.1, rstan 2.12.1 and StanHeaders 2.12.0. (The only two R installations on my machine that have rstan and StanHeaders installed.)

I followed the suggestions in the thread started by Dieter Menne, removing and re-installing StanHeaders and rstan multiple times.  Finally I realised that the stan() command had a "verbose=TRUE" option.  Once I used this, I could spot the problem immediately (slowly stopping kicking myself for not realising this earlier :) ).  See the two attached files which try to compile the school example from rstan's vignette on my machine, once using the 32-bit version and once the 64 bit version.  Both files state:

    >> setting environment variables:
    PKG_LIBS =  -L'/opt/R/R-3.3.2/lib/R/library/StanHeaders/lib' -lStanHeaders

and these values are later used in a "g++ -shared" (or "g++ -m32 -shared") command.  But on my machine:

    berwin@ECM-DTC-716:~$ locate libStanHeaders
    /opt/R/R-3.3.1/lib/R/library/StanHeaders/lib/32/libStanHeaders.a
    /opt/R/R-3.3.1/lib/R/library/StanHeaders/lib/64/libStanHeaders.a
    /opt/R/R-3.3.2/lib/R/library/StanHeaders/lib/32/libStanHeaders.a
    /opt/R/R-3.3.2/lib/R/library/StanHeaders/lib/64/libStanHeaders.a

So it is no surprise that the linker cannot find the StanHeaders library.

I guess a fix for the moment is to link "/opt/R/R-3.3.2/lib/R/library/StanHeaders/lib/64/libStanHeaders.a" to "/opt/R/R-3.3.2/lib/R/library/StanHeaders/lib/libStanHeaders.a" and not use rstan with the 32 bit architecture.

The only place in rstan's sources that I could find that seem to relate to the above output of environment variables is in the function 'rstanplugin' defined in "plugin.R":

    if (.Platform$OS.type == "windows")
      StanHeaders_pkg_libs <- system.file("libs", .Platform$r_arch, package = "StanHeaders")
    else StanHeaders_pkg_libs <- system.file("lib", package = "StanHeaders")

I must admit that I am a bit puzzled by this code.  Why is the architecture only taken into account if R is run on a Windows platform?

Wishing you all a Happy New Year!

Cheers,

Berwin

messages.body_plain:
> On Dec 30, 2016, at 2:02 PM, Phil Price <pnp...@creekcats.com> wrote:
>
>
> By the way, Bob (or others on the Stan team) I'd like to put in a plug for adding the functions floor(), ceiling(), and maybe round() to the language. I am mimicking these with a while loop that counts through integers until it exceeds the number I'm interested in -- and it was an embarrassing mistake in doing this that led to my off-by-one problem, but of course that's no one's fault but mine. But it's still a pain to have to program this everywhere I need it, and it hurts readability, and...well, basically there's a good reason pretty much every other language lets you find the integer part of a number.

This is an ongoing request we receive all the time.  There
are warnings in the manual around places where we do allow it.

We do allow you to get the floating point integer part
of a number, but that's not useful for indexing.  And even
that we shouldn't do, as the derivative's a step function
whereas HMC is assuming a continuously differentiable log density.

That's why we didn't add the versions as is.  We may get rid
of the ability to do what you're trying to do in the future.

> Also, although it's not a big deal to count to 90 when trying to find the greatest integer less than 90.3, it is certainly inefficient...and what if I am working with, say, a year of 1-second data (not at all an unrealistic possibility...indeed, I may soon be working with years worth of 1/120-second data!). I'm not going to count to 27 million to find the integer part of 27,000,000.63.  There must be a super-fast way to do this... find a range and then use bisection, perhaps? Maybe there's something really simple that should be obvious to me but isn't. But why make me jump through any of these hoops at all? Please, put real --> int conversion into the language.

Binary search will do it in log(n) time.  We don't want to
make it hard and provide hoops, we want to discourage it altogether
in favor of continuous models (or marginalized discrete models).

Of course, everyone who wants to code this kind of thing just tells
us we should make it easier, as you did.

- Bob

>
> Huh?  Stan has these functions!  See page 420-421 of the Stan 2.14.0 manual!  (And the functions are not new to version 2.14.)

They return real values, not integers, so you can't use
them as indexes.  That's intentional.  Each one is linked
to a warning because it doesn't have continuous derivatives.
Which means it will break HMC unless used very carefully (as
in some kinds of interpolations).

messages.body_plain:
Nothing jumps out at me here for either efficiency or
coding.  But I'm not familiar with some of these parameterizations.

When you say it estimates all parameters other than phi, you
mean it recovers them in the appropriate posterior intervals over
simulated data?  What happens to phi?  This can sometimes happen
when the model's not identified, which will cause wide posterior
intervals on the non-identified parameter and slow sampling (even
if it's technically identified softly by a prior but not the likelihood).

This kind of thing is dangerous:

	sigma_y = sigma_y_norm / sqrt(sigma_y_raw);

as you're building in a non-identifiability between sigma_y_norm
and sigma_y_raw (if they both go up, sigma_y stays the same).

And we don't recommend these hard constraints on parameters

	real<lower=1, upper=80> nu_sigma_y;
...
	nu_sigma_y ~ gamma(2, 0.1);

You can vectorize that final normal sample, but that's unlikely
to be the bottleneck.  For even more efficiency, you could group
the data by s[t] so you could share scale parameters---but as I
said, I doubt the normal is the bottleneck here.

How are the n_eff for the correlation Cholesky factor?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
MCMC is more robust than ADVI or MAP and also computes
the reference result.  ADVI is an approximation, but the
code's not very robust in Stan to fit.  MAP computes something
different, and a MAP solution might not exist in many cases
(like hierarchical models) where the posterior mode is well
defined.

What do you mean by "instantiation" when you say it's a pain?
Initialization?  Did you try default inits?

All of HMC, ADVI, and L-BFGS use gradient information, but
the algorithms are totally different.  Also, ADVI isn't very
robust.  And L-BFGS won't find a mode where one doesn't
exist.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Yes.  No idea what's going on with phi then.  Are you sure
you're not getting the right answer?  That is, maybe the right
answer is very little time series effect based on previous value.

Isolating phi, you give it a prior

  phi ~ normal(0,1);

and use it to generate epsilon[t] with a negative phi[s[t]] * y[t - 1]
term:

  for (t in 2:T)
    epsilon[t] = y[t] - (mu[s[t]] + y_temp[t] + phi[s[t]] * y[t-1]);

And then it shows up in the linear predictor as

  for (t in 2:T)
    y[t] ~ normal(mu[s[t]]
                    + y_temp[t]
                    + phi[s[t]] * y[t - 1]
                    + theta[s[t]] * epsilon[t - 1],
                  sigma_y[s[t]]);

If you expand out epsilon[t-1], you get:

   y[t] ~ normal(mu[s[t]]
                   + t_temp[t]
                   + phi[s[t]] * y[t - 1]
                   + theta[s[t]] * (y[t - 1]
                                    - mu[s[t - 1]]
                                    - y_temp[t] +
                                    - phi[s[t - 1]] * y[t-2])),
                  sigma_y[s[t]]);

where

  y_temp = rows_dot_product(x, beta[s]);

So you get two terms in y[t - 1] and one in y[t - 2] that
may be close to canceling each other out:

  phi[s[t]] * y[t - 1]

  - theta[s[t]] * y[t - 1]

  - theta[s[t]] * phi[s[t - 1]] * y[t - 2]

So the question is whether you're recovering the parameters from
simulated data within the posterior intervals.  And if not, it may
be the identifiability issues raised from the above (phi[s[t]] and
theta[s[t]] are strongly anti-correlated and if y[t - 1] and y[t - 2]
are similar and s[t] and s[t - 1] are similar, it's going to cause
another kind of cancellation.

- Bob

P.S.  Tabs in code are bad news, especially when mixed with spaces.

What happens under random inits?   Do you get -infinity log
density?  Or does it fail with an exception somewhere?  The
latter usually indicates a bug in the coding, usually missing
constraints on parameters.  All parameter values satisfying
the declared constraints should have support (finite log density)
in the model.

The other common problem in GPs is lack of jitter---trying to make
the model too deterministic.

You need to balance parens.  I don't know what you were intending, but the
caret's pointing at the problem after the first multi_normal_lpdf --- what
did you expect commas to do, add? I'd suggest writing in a format
that makes that obvious and doesn't use such long lines

  for (n in 1:N)

    target += log(prior_pi[1])

      + multi_normal_lpdf(trajectory[n] | mu_model_1, Sigma_model_1)

      + log(prior_pi[2])

      + multi_normal_lpdf(trajectory[n] | mu_model_2, Sigma_model_2)

      + log(prior_pi[3])
      + multi_student_t_log(trajectory[n], nu, mu_model_3, Sigma_model_3);

But my guess is that you wanted to implement a mixture model, in
which case you need t put those three components in (1, 2, and 3) into
a vector ps of size 3 and call

  target += log_sum_exp(ps);

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I was trying to run a certain multilevel model and I wanted to compare the results of using one, two, or three levels in the model. For that, I added a data variable called n_levels and, in the model, added if/elses that change the model depending on whether n_levels = 1, 2, or 3. However, when n_levels = 1 or 2, convergence of the actually used parametres is terrible, often with Rhat > 40. After fiddling with it, I found out that the mere fact of adding extraneous parametres (without using them for anything) seems to worsen convergence considerably.

Why does it happen? Is it avoidable?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I experienced a couple of issues while trying to build a package on Windows:

1. Rstantools creates a skeleton with cleanup.win file that contains call to sed
  sed -i.bak '/current_statement_begin__ = [0-9]/d' src/include/models.hpp
The problem is that on Windows, GNU sed will change permissions (drastically reduce them)  of the edited file, making  models.hpp unreachable
Modules.cpp:3:30: fatal error: include/models.hpp: Permission denied
It is apparently a well known bug of sed, e.g. https://cygwin.com/ml/cygwin/2012-02/msg00616.html

2. In DESCRIPTION file methods have minimum specified as (>= 3.4.0), but there is no such thing on Windows, the latest method is of version 3.3.2. I noticed that in rstanarm's DESCROPTION file there is no minimum.

Regards,
Slawek

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problem with missing covariates
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Problem with missing covariates
messages.body_plain:
You shouldn't need to use the missing variables in the model block.
If you think you need to model the missing data as parameters so
that you can use those parameters in inference, you don't need them.
Imputing the missing values then using them in the fit won't change
the fit.  (Sometimes they can in semi-supervised learning problems
where the outcome is missing but the covariates are observed.)

Stan doesn't allow discrete parameters, so there's no way to
generate them in the model block without really ugly and inefficient
hacks that we very strongly discourage.

- Bob

I have the filling that imputing the missing values and using them in one program might not change the fit. However, consider the following artificial data set:

X1 X2 X3 Y
1 NA 0 4
2 NA 1 5
3 NA 1 7
4 1 NA 5

If we want to regress Y on X2 and X3 (binary variable) and if we do not do any thing for X2 and X3 then we have nothing to do because in all case either X2 or X3 are missing.

That is why I really want that Stan can help me to impute (or generate) and the re-use the imputed values in the regression model.

For continuous variables everything is OK because I can specify the missing values as parameters. Unfortunately, I have to work with binary data.

Kind regards,
Tran.

There is no such option in rstanarm because the models are precompiled. You can certainly specify a prior mean and prior standard deviation such that zero is three or four standard deviations below the prior mean, in which case it is very unlikely that much of the posterior mass would be below zero.

Alternatively, I think you can do constraints like that in brms or certainly if you write the Stan program yourself.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

This should be easy to do. Maybe the ascii math is not so obvious, but what you need to do is to integrate log(y_n) for the nth state of the ODE instead of y_n. To do that take you current ODE system

dy_n/dt = f(y_1, ... y_n, ...)

then divide the n-th ODE rhs by y_n, so you get

1/y_n dy_n/dt = dly_n/dt =  f(y_1, ... y_n, ...)/y_n

This will make your states y_n to be log-states ly_n=log(y_n). All you have to do now is to transform from the log(y_n) to y_n just before the ODE rhs in the functor which you wrote in Stan. That's it.

However, there is a catch here - calculating things on the log scale means that you cannot represent a 0. You can only represent values close to zero which is something to consider when initializing. So you will have to call 10^-5 or something like that to be zero; which number here makes sense depends on your problem specifics. Do not make this number crazy small as this will make the system terribly hard to solve (going from nothing to something is a huge jump on the log-scale).

Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
But so will numerical errors, both from the approximate ODE solvers
and floating point arithmetic.  The point is that if you are trying to
solve an ODE system whose states are positive but are very close
to zero then you are much better off working in log space.

I agree with Paul that this is not often useful. Unless the lower=0 constraint is a logical requirement (e.g. variances must have lower=0) it's usually better to impose soft constraints via a prior that places little weight on negative values (as Ben suggested). If there really is a constraint that is absolutely necessary then, judging from what Paul said, it should be simple to try brms for that.

2. Both sum_alpha and sum(alpha) are different variables. sum_alpha is fixed and sum(alpha) is the sum of all current alphas.

3. I have now Cholesky decomposed (beta[n] * sum_beta * Sigma[k] / sum(beta)) to chol_Sigma_k. And Sigma[k] is constructed from a correlation matrix (=H_prime_inv_corr) in the 'transformed parameters' block. I was not successful in applying the LKJ prior over H_prime_inv_corr and therefore I pass H_prime_inv_corr into Stan (via the data{}).

The code now takes in 1000 cells and more than 25 genes. No errors, there is convergence. Currently I have this running on 1000 cells and 50 genes.  Would you have any suggestions for optimising the current code?
My next step is to get the code handle 3000 cells and 500 genes.

Regards,
Sandhya

On Thursday, 22 December 2016 10:13:49 UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> You want to use a Cholesky factor parameterization of
> a covariance matrix.  Then it'll require some footwork to
> do the modifications you do:
>
>     GaussLogLike[k] = log (pi_z[k]) + multi_normal_lpdf(X[n]|
>                                    ((alpha[n]*sum_alpha)*mu[k])/sum(alpha),
>                                         ((beta[n]*sum_beta)*Sigma[k])/sum(beta));
>
> The more I read these messages, the more I think our users
> must have defective space keys on their keyboards!  I'd write this as:
>
>     gauss_ll[k] = log(pi_z[k])
>                 + multi_normal_lpdf(X[n] | alpha[n] * sum_alpha /sum(alpha) * mu[k],
>                                            beta[n] * sum_beta / sum(beta) * Sigma[k]);
>
> The reason I reordered is that it's better to do all the scalar
> arithmetic together to reduce the number of scalar * matrix multiplies.
> Arithmetic operators are all left associative
> (i.e., (a * b / c) == ((a * b) / c)).
>
> Presumably, contrary to the naming, sum_alpha != sum(alpha) --- otherwise
> just drop them all.  You'll have to figure out how to calculate the Cholesky
> factor of of beta[n] * sum_beta * Sigma[k] / sum(beta) from the Cholesky factor
>  of Sigma.
>
> I don't understand why you'd want to overparameterize like this, but the
> above is what you'll need to do to make it efficient.
>
> We generally use a scaled correlation matrix with an LKJ prior on the correlation
> matrix.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Problem with missing covariates
messages.body_plain:
If you have to impute discrete data, then you
can often do it one observation at a time, in
which case the marginalization will be tractable.

You'll need to provide a probability model
for log p(X1, X2, X3, Y) and presumably that's just

SUM_n log p(X1[n], X2[n], X3[n], Y[n])

Then marginalize out the necessary X's on the inside.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, January 11, 2017 at 3:28:49 PM UTC-5, Stephen Martin wrote:
> I'll fill out a feature request, but just two questions before I do.
>
> 1) Why can I not add (literally) two mcmc plots together ala ggplot like: mcmc_dens(stanOut,pars='theta') + mcmc_dens(stanOut,pars='theta2); ggplot allows such things when adding geoms, but bayesplot says: Error: Don't know how to add o to a plot

This isn't bayesplot specific. It's just that ggplot2 lets you add geoms to ggplot objects but not ggplot objects to ggplot objects. For example:

library(ggplot2)
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100), y = rnorm(100))
p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(x,y)) + geom_point()
p1

p1 + geom_line() # works because adding geom to ggplot object

p2 <- ggplot(d, aes(x,y)) + geom_line()
p1 + p2 # errors because adding ggplot object to ggplot object

>
> 2) I'm not sure how bayesplot does the by-variable faceting or plotting (when plotting densities of several variables, one plot is made with a 'row' per variable), but why does + facet_null() not nullify this faceting? (I assume because internally it's not using faceting?)

Which bayesplot function are you referring to? The way the faceting is done varies a bit. With mcmc_dens, for example, I think facet_null should nullify the faceting, for example:

library(bayesplot)
x <- example_mcmc_draws()
mcmc_dens(x) # this uses facet_wrap internally
mcmc_dens(x) + facet_null() # nullifies the faceting

Jonah

Any suggestions are most welcome.

Gene Quinn

Stonehill College

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] pystan or rstan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] pystan or rstan
messages.body_plain:
I'm surprised we don't get this question a lot, but I guess people
usually choose their language first, then look for packages in it.

PyStan and RStan Both call the same basic C++ code in Stan to do inference.

The ecosystem around RStan is much larger than around PyStan (packages like
ShinyStan, loo, RStanArm, and BayesPlot), but we'd love to have
some people train people in PyStan who could help close the gap!

You can see a basic Jupyter tutorial in Python
that Chris Fonnesbeck put together here:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/radon.html

So you can see that you get all the basic sampling and plotting
you need directly in PyStan (and other Python packages).

- Bob

P.S.  "Stan" isn't an acronym, so we prefer "Stan" to "STAN".  It's named
      after Stanislaw Ulam.

messages.subject: conceptual question about including a numerical integration step inside an mcmc
messages.subject_clean: conceptual question about including a numerical integration step inside an mcmc
messages.body_plain:
Hi, i have a known form for a population model likelihood for a known response, y,  that I will adjust through multiplications of quantities dependent on known sampling weights, w, and model parameters with the purpose to provide consistent estimation of the population model parameters estimated on a sample realized from an informative sampling design.   One of the multiplicative quantities that adjusts the population likelihood must be computed by a numerical integration step - to compute an expectation  - on each MCMC iteration. The integration is of an expression that is a function of known sampling weights, w, and response values, y, which are both known,  and is also a function of model parameters.  The integration is taken with respect to the scalar response variable, y.   I don't believe this type of set-up may be accommodated by stan (after exploring the manual), but write to ask and be sure.

Thanks for your response,

Terrance

--
Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] rstan 2.14 doesn't accept data.frames, causes compile error.
messages.body_plain:
I'd rather fix the input format and have programs on the
outside conform to that.  It's much much easier for us to maintain
and doc, and the interfaces are easier to understand.

I do understand that this goes against a lot of the R philosophy of trying
to guess what a client wants and then trying to munge data structures to
accomplish it with implicit conversions.  Even simple things are problematic,
such as whether a size-one container and scalar are the same thing:

  > a = c(5)

  > b = 5

  > a == b
  [1] TRUE

Underlyingly, Stan is statically typed and treats integers and reals
as separate, and containers and scalars as spearate types.

- Bob

> after finishing the code for a regression model of a time series with autoregressive errors, I would now like to extend this to a VAR. I was thinking about a model of M time series with a lag of P and which includes some exogenous input(s) C, and, besides I would like to make a hierarchical model for J subjects of it. This has all been coded before by Rob Trangucci and Ryan Batt (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/PmGMnqXRD28/AnXr4IVOAgAJ) and I have taken the biggest part of the code from there. Ben Goodrich has also shown a way to code for a correlation matrix for specific subsets of units in a series (see https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/6khmjLtF5I0) which was adopted by Jim Savage. The presented code is thus just my attempt to add all together and make it more general. It also works alright when done with a bunch of for loops generating the coefficients I simulated in an R script, although it is very slow  - as to be expected. The problem I am facing is how to get the model to run efficiently. I have tried to vectorize most of what was easy to do and to apply the nonparametric reparametrization but I am struggling with the access to the matrices especially when there are arrays of matrices. For example, I am trying to estimate z_B as a vector from an array of [P, J, M, M] .
>
> for (p in 1:P){
>   for (j in 1:J)
>     to_vector(z_beta[p,j]) ~ normal(0,1);
> }

You haven't told us what z_beta is.  Was z_B meant to be z_beta?
And I don't know what array of P, J, M, M means --- is it a 4D
data structure with sizes P, J, M, and M?

>
> This here is not only ugly, it also produces just nans.

Have you defined z_beta?  The sampling notation doesn't sample, it just
increments the log density, so you need to have z_beta defined before
you call the above line.

> But even looking in the manual and previous post I can't get my head around how to do this.

See the manual, section 4.3, Sampling Statements.

>
>
> The second thing I should optimize is the multinormal distribution. A vectorized form would make the estimation much faster but when I change
>
> for(t in 1:(T-P))
>     Y_obs[t] ~ multi_normal(mus[t], covar[s_obs[t]]);
>
> to
>
> Y_obs ~ multi_normal(mus, covar[s_obs]);

Look at the available signatures.  Y_obs and mus can be
either vectors or arrays of vectors.

> it doesn't work and I can't figure out a way to get covariance as a KxK matrix from the KxKxJ array . Of course, another possibility would be to use the Cholesky decomposition but I have not been able to get this running at all.

We can't help if we don't know what you tried.

The biggest thing you can do for efficiency and stability is
move to a Cholesky factor parameterization.

> It basically boils down to the question how to include a matrix coming from an array of matrices, I think.

Won't work.  We don't allow vectorization of the covariance.  But
it wouldn't help anyway, even if we did, because the advantage of
vectorization here is only having to factor the matrix once.

What you could do is collect all of the cases with s_obs[t] = k,
which can then share a covariance matrix.

- Bob

> On Jan 10, 2017, at 3:53 PM, Sandhya Prabhakaran <sandhyapr...@gmail.com> wrote:

> 1. I have tidied up the GaussLogLike[k], as per your suggestion. We wish to account for cell (=observation)-wise scalings and therefore have alphas and betas as scalings for the mean and covariance of the Gaussian, respectively.

Now I get what you're trying to do.  You have different counts
in the correlated multinomial you're trying to approximate.

The way I would go about this (other than working on the natural
scale rather than this approximation), would be to have a single
scaling fixed by the data that applies to both the mean and
the covariance matrix.

> 2. Both sum_alpha and sum(alpha) are different variables. sum_alpha is fixed and sum(alpha) is the sum of all current alphas.
>
> 3. I have now Cholesky decomposed (beta[n] * sum_beta * Sigma[k] / sum(beta)) to chol_Sigma_k. And Sigma[k] is constructed from a correlation matrix (=H_prime_inv_corr) in the 'transformed parameters' block. I was not successful in applying the LKJ prior over H_prime_inv_corr and therefore I pass H_prime_inv_corr into Stan (via the data{}).

What happened?  You want to use a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix
as the data type, then give it an LKJ-Cholesky prior, then scale the
mean and the Cholesky factor, and you should be good to go.  That way,
you work on the standard deviation scale, which has the same units as the mean.

Otherwise, you seem to have too many degrees of freedom to fit this well.

> The code now takes in 1000 cells and more than 25 genes. No errors, there is convergence. Currently I have this running on 1000 cells and 50 genes.  Would you have any suggestions for optimising the current code?

Neat.  Can you send the whole current program?

How long does it take and what's the resulting n_eff?  Do multiple
chains converge to the same solution?

- Bob

Turns out you were correct in saying that working directly on the log-scale can make the arithmetic more robust. Specifically, the Cholesky parametrized normal likelihood was the issue, and using the following representation directly (dropping the 2pi constant) lets the model run (even with opt, haven't tried out vb yet though will report back when I do). I wonder if this was a problem with using the Sigma = LL' factorization when L didn't have positive diagonal entries, and therefore wasn't the _Cholesky_ factorization, even though the math could be the same. If Stan assumes that the diagonal elements are positive, the log determinant could be computed more efficiently (see below: the square in L_ii^2 could be brought out of the sum as a scaling factor). In that case, taking the log of L_ii could be undefined (in the real plane) and return infinity or something. Does Stan do this under the hood?

> > This class is about 50% cs majors who aren't really interested in learning R, but need to learn Python.  The rest of the class is mostly environmental science and biology, and I think they would benefit from an introduction to Python as well.

Indeed. But as a mid- to long-term investment rather than a short-term commodity acquisition (see below)...

> >
> > My main concern is getting the software to work in a diverse hardware/OS environment.  Maybe 60-65% of the students have macs, but the others have windows.
> >
> > Any suggestions are most welcome.
>
> If you have a few hundred dollars or your students have a few dollars, I would suggest doing a course like that through Sage Math Cloud
>
> https://cloud.sagemath.com/help#

Nice idea. But a few caveats :

1) Sage is Python2-based ; this will change over time, but is a large task (in good way, but not yet here). This might be an hindrance if your students have been introduced to Python3 only, as it is likely nowadays.

On the other hand, introducing CS students to the necessities (and difficulties) of maintaining backward compatibility might be a Good Thing For Them(TM)...

2) Sage's R version is 3.2.4 ; it's in the process of being updated, but R's new dependance on an external SSL library opened a few cans of worms (mostly pseudo-legal concerns about what amounts in practice to a dependance on OpenSSL, which ruffles a few feathers...). The recent OpenSSL 1.1 tragicomedy has complicated things again (make that a crate of canned worms...), making upgrading Python the #1 priority (this done as of yesterday).

This should change soon (not as soon as I wished), but don't hold your breath : I'm on it since the end of last spring...

3) For practical purposes, R is (currently) vastly more useful to a biostatistician, a biologist, an ecologist or a physician than Python : almost 10 000 R packages have been developed over time, that cover an awful lot of applied statistical practice (and folklore (and prehistory)) ; this has also given R a reputation among journal reviewers, who aren't so keen to dispute an R package  worthiness as to scrutinize (suspiciously) a home-cooked Python program.

Bob (below) notes that the existence of (a lot of) Stan support R packages is a point to consider. He's right...

This also may change over time, given what is thought of as the "cleanliness" of Python over the "scruffy" nature of R (which is really Scheme with another syntax), which makes mastering it more an art than a science. But, again, it is not there yet.

>
>
> They have rstan already but would pip install pystan for you. I would use it for my own class but the students are more comfortable with RStudio than Jupyter.

I found cloud.sagemath.com <http://cloud.sagemath.com>'s staff extremely helpful and eager to help even users of "freebee" accounts. Installing pystan should be no problem (as long as your account has Internet access...). Ditto for rstan and its support packages.

Introducing various interfaces to your students should also be a Good Thing For Them(TM). Consider also R's interface to Jupyter (a. k. a. IRkernel), and maybe emacs+(markdown|LaTeX) (irreplaceable for serious work, such as publication...).

cloud.sagemath.com <http://cloud.sagemath.com> also offers a LaTeX editor claiming to have collaboration features, such as incremental compilation. I have no idea of its valu, being an emacs die-hard...

HTH,

--
Emmanuel Charpentier

>
> Ben

messages.body_plain:
Look at the manual chapter on transforms.
In the simplest case, the lower-bound transform
can depend on data.  But it drops out because
it's constant on the log scale.  You can see this
in the math written out there.  Basicaly, the data
shows up as a term, but if after you compute the
log Jacobian, you can drop additive constants.

The bigger question is why are you putting a distribution
on a function of parameters?  Usually we want to think
generatively and only wind up doing something like you suggest
if there's an underlying generative model that we transform
for some computational advantage, such as a non-centered
reparameterization of hierarchical models.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I was talking to Michael Betancourt, who was suggesting that
you use an independent Poisson approximations to the large
count multinomial rather than a multinormal because the covariance
vanishes in the multinomial as the count goes up (intuitively, when
there are only a few counts, you get negative correlations by
construction, which dampen as you get more independent counts).

Apparently, it's what physicists have been doing for years.  There
are a gazillion hits for a search on Google, but I don't know which
one to recommend---some look very theoretical.  This one seems clear:

https://www.jstor.org/stable/3314676

If N is the number of trials and theta the simplex of distributions
and we have

  X ~ Multinomial(N, theta)

then

  E[X[n]] = N * theta[n]

and we can approximate

  Multinomial(X | N, theta)

  ~approx~

  PROD_k Poisson(X[k] | N * theta[k])

In vectorized Stan notation, that'd just be

  X ~ poisson(N * theta);

The other advantage is that it's much more efficient to compute n Poissons
than a multivariate normal, so the scaling should be much better.

- Bob

Dear Bob,

Thanks for getting back.

Why we used the Gaussian likelihood: Although we get a count matrix (with cells as rows and genes as columns), we log transform the data so that we can work in the continuous (Gaussian) space. This was further vetted by using the Lilliefors test (to confirm the Gaussianity assumption) on real data.

The reason we use separate scalings for the moments was also dictated by the data. (In our paper, Section 2, paragraph titled ‘Motivations for cell-specific scalings’). The \alphas that scale the means capture the library-size variation (rowsums of the data matrix) whereas the \betas that scale the covariances capture larger noise in cells that have a smaller library size.

Regarding the Poisson likelihood: I shall go through the 'Poisson approximation to multinomial' paper. So here you mean to say that we use a Poisson likelihood instead of a multivariate Gaussian. Yes, I agree and am up for converting the model. This should seem easier as well. Although, our current aim is to get, at least the model we presented in ICML to run with the data of 3000 cells x 500 genes in Stan. We do have R/Matlab code that implements the MCMC/Gibbs. This was taking a much longer time to converge and therefore we decided to go down the Stan route.

Runtime: 1000 cells x 15 genes takes less than an hour. The inferred labels are quite close to the true labels. By ‘multiple chains converging’ did you mean ‘multiple independent runs’? If so, yes, the independent runs do give similar clustering results.
I am currently running 3000 cells x 25 genes and this has been running for > 12 hours.
Do you think it is going to be hard to scale the current model to handle 500 or more genes. I understand that we can scale the number of cells using the subsampling that ADVI can use (via minibatch scaling factor). I have not tried this yet.

Let me code up the model again with the LKJ prior.

> I was talking to Michael Betancourt, who was suggesting that
> you use an independent Poisson approximations to the large
> count multinomial rather than a multinormal because the covariance
> vanishes in the multinomial as the count goes up (intuitively, when
> there are only a few counts, you get negative correlations by
> construction, which dampen as you get more independent counts).
>
> Apparently, it's what physicists have been doing for years.  There
> are a gazillion hits for a search on Google, but I don't know which
> one to recommend---some look very theoretical.  This one seems clear:
>
> https://www.jstor.org/stable/3314676
>
> If N is the number of trials and theta the simplex of distributions
> and we have
>
>   X ~ Multinomial(N, theta)
>
> then
>
>   E[X[n]] = N * theta[n]
>
> and we can approximate
>
>   Multinomial(X | N, theta)
>
>   ~approx~
>
>   PROD_k Poisson(X[k] | N * theta[k])
>
> In vectorized Stan notation, that'd just be
>
>   X ~ poisson(N * theta);
>
> The other advantage is that it's much more efficient to compute n Poissons
> than a multivariate normal, so the scaling should be much better.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Understanding stan_betareg
messages.subject_clean: Understanding stan_betareg
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm quite new to bayesian modeling, and in that regard I appreciate rstanarm a lot, since it makes bayesian methods way more approachable.

In order to get estimates and uncertainty intervals for a proportion I was trying out stan_betareg by simulating fake data. From what I understand (which might be wrong), I can calculate the mean of a beta distribution with mean = alpha / (alpha + beta). I simulated data with rbeta for different groups and sample sizes and tried to recover their means by using stan_betareg(y ~ 0 + group, ..). I transformed the resulting coefficients with arm::invlogit, so I could interpret them on the probability scale. As far as I understand it, my true means should fall 9 out of 10 times within a 90% interval from tidy(stanreg) or using mcmc_recover_intervals.

Unfortunately I was unsuccessful with my attempts. The true mean fell only 52 out of 100 times within the interval. Especially for a group with simulated data from rbeta(n, 34, 6), the estimate was always off. Most likely I'm misunderstanding, what I am estimating with beta regression, and how I should treat the resulting coefficients. If you could give me any pointers on what I'm missing, I'd appreciate it a lot.

I used the following code:

library(tidyverse)
library(rstanarm)
library(broom)

sim_setup <- data_frame(
  group = letters[1:5],
  alpha = c(4, 4, 34, 1, .6),
  beta = c(4, 2, 6, 3, .9),
  size = c(10, 40, 70, 150, 300)
) %>%
  mutate(mean = alpha / (alpha + beta))

# simulation
true <- sim_setup$mean

simulate_data <- function(setup) {
  setup %>%
    by_row(~rbeta(.$size, .$alpha, .$beta)) %>%
    unnest(y = .out)
}

find_values <- function(data) {
  bayes <- stan_betareg(y ~ 0 + group, data, iter = 400)

  tidy(bayes, intervals = T) %>%
    dplyr::select(-std.error) %>%
    filter(term != "(phi)") %>%
    dmap_if(is_numeric, arm::invlogit) %>%
    mutate(hit = case_when(true < .$lower | true > .$upper ~ FALSE,
                           TRUE ~ TRUE))
}

sim_res <- rerun(20, simulate_data(sim_setup)) %>%
  map(find_values)

sim_res_collected <- sim_res %>%
  bind_rows(.id = "id") %>%
  mutate(true = rep(true, 20),
         id = factor(id, levels = 1:20))

sim_res_collected %>% count(hit)

ggplot(sim_res_collected, aes(term, estimate, ymin = lower, ymax = upper)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_point(aes(y = true), colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~id) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Results from 20 simulation draws")

First, it is easy to confuse yourself if you average over simulated datasets. Bayesian methods should work fine in this frequentist setting but that is because they work fine on each simulated dataset, which is what Bayesians should care about in practice.

Second, any X% credible interval should have a X / 100 probability of containing the true value, but we don't like X = 90 because the endpoints are not estimated very precisely. This is compounded when you only do 400 iterations and keep 200 of them; stick with the defaults.

Third, the usual way to evaluate something like this is to simulate one dataset, obtain the posterior distribution, obtain the posterior predictive distribution, and  check what proportion of the observations in the one dataset fall within some quantiles of the posterior predictive distribution for each observation. In your case, it would look like

dat <- simulate_data(sim_setup)
post <- stan_betareg(y ~ 0 + group, data = dat)
PPD <- posterior_predict(post)
Qs <- apply(PPD, 2, FUN = quantile, probs = c(0.25, 0.75))
mean(dat$y > Qs[1,] & dat$y < Qs[2,]) # usually a little more than 0.5

It is true that posterior_interval(post, prob = 0.5) reflects a belief that the true parameters (in log-odds) are contained within these intervals with probability 0.5, but you are not going to have the true parameters to verify that with real data. But you will always have the data, so you can always check whether the posterior predictions of the data are well-calibrated.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
In Stan, what's saved and not is part of the language. There are a few controls in the interfaces, but let's start with fundamentals.

Variables declared in parameters, transformed parameters, and generated quantities are saved. Exception: variables declared in local blocks within those blocks. Variables declared within the model block, transformed data block, or any local blocks are not saved. There's no way to get them out of an interface if they've been declared there.

To save those parameters, I'll walk through steps for just one of them.

1. Move the declaration of g_a_0 from the model block to the transformed parameters block.
2. Move the definition, g_a_0 <- xi_a * mu_a_raw;, from the model block to the transformed data block.

That's it. Now g_a_0 will be in the output. There are other ways to do this, but this is probably the most straightforward.

Daniel

Part of your problem is that you chose an example that does not run. We'll fix it, but if you are having trouble getting started, you can estimate hierarchical models like this using the rstanarm or brms R packages via lme4-style syntax. In the radon case, it would be something like

radon <- rstan::read_rdump("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stan-dev/example-models/master/ARM/Ch.17/17.1_radon_wishart2.data.R")

library(rstanarm)
posterior <- stan_lmer(y ~ x + (1 + x | county), data = radon)

Ben

> On Jan 14, 2017, at 8:06 AM, Samuel Hinton <samue...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Daniel,
>
> Thanks for the heads up about the name, Im used to just assuming the acronym!
>
> And I understand about providing a code example, at the moment I don't have a smaller reproduction, just the full model found at https://github.com/dessn/sn-bhm/blob/master/dessn/models/d_simple_stan/approx_mass/model.stan (but Ill try and create a toy example, because I dont expect anyone to go through that big model). As to what I am unable to put into stan, it is a high dimensional integral that appears on the denominator of the likelihood, not the numerator, so the standard way of marginalising over parameters doesn't won't work. If there is a way to put a theta-dependent integral on the denominator of the joint lpdf I would be very happy to break free of my ignorance!
>
> I will create a toy model asap and update this post with it, but in the meantime perhaps I can make my enquiry about the joint lpdf distribution clearer.
>
> The plot I included is just a trace plot of the joint lpdf (what I called the posterior) subtracted from the max value of the joint lpdf. It is sorted by another parameter (which is responsible for the trend). What I was inquiring about was the distribution of the points. For example, if the chains from Stan are equally weighted, it seems that it has sampled points with a joint lpdf of around -200 far more than points which have a joint lpdf between 0 and -100. This is confusing to me, as I thought the higher the joint lpdf, the more samples one should get. Does that make my confusion/position any easier to understand?

Yes.  And it's what you want.  Stan's MCMC *samples* from the posterior,
it doesn't optimize it.

Here's a simple example you can recreate in R without Stan using
only simple Monte Carlo sampling.  Suppose you have bernoulli(0.7)
and you draw 100 samples.  Most of those samples are going
to have around 70 successes in them even though 100 successes
had *much* higher probability.

For instance, 50 replication of 100 draws with a 70% chance of
success.

> rbinom(50, 100, 0.7)
 [1] 65 79 66 75 73 69 63 69 73 71 68 72 65 77 68 73 64 71 61 68 76 72 75 72 74
[26] 78 65 67 72 65 67 69 63 76 76 70 72 75 72 69 66 71 75 66 70 62 58 76 69 64

See how none of them are near 100?

- Bob

> I totally agree with you Bob. What I am trying to do is not generative rather an attempt to inform the inference about a joint behavior of data and parameters being estimated.

That's a tricky business in both statistical and computational
terms, and it will make your model a lot harder for people
to understand.

The standard thing to do is put constraints on the parameters
through the prior alone.  You can define the prior in terms of
transforms of the parameters, but then you need a Jacobian.

- Bob

>

>
> On Friday, January 13, 2017 at 12:37:46 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Look at the manual chapter on transforms.
> In the simplest case, the lower-bound transform
> can depend on data.  But it drops out because
> it's constant on the log scale.  You can see this
> in the math written out there.  Basicaly, the data
> shows up as a term, but if after you compute the
> log Jacobian, you can drop additive constants.
>
> The bigger question is why are you putting a distribution
> on a function of parameters?  Usually we want to think
> generatively and only wind up doing something like you suggest
> if there's an underlying generative model that we transform
> for some computational advantage, such as a non-centered
> reparameterization of hierarchical models.

messages.body_plain:
Yes, the determinant calculation for the Cholesky-parameterized
multi-normal is done efficiently.  Ben keeps a close watch on
our linear algebra for critical functions like this.

The relevant code for the determinant is in

  stan/math/prim/mat/prob/multi_normal_cholesky_lpdf.hpp

and looks just like you'd expect for Cholesky factor L and
log density accumulator lp (recall the determinant is in
the denominator of the density).

        lp -= L.diagonal().array().log().sum() * size_vec;

size_vec is the number of variates, so that we only compute
this determinant once if it's called with an array of
variates.  That is, if we call y ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L) and y
is an array of vectors.  Then rather than computing it and adding
it for each vector element of y, we just multiply.

Also, we use template traits programming to wrap this in a static
conditional that only includes the decrement if the matrix L
isn't data.  If it's data, the result is a constant term and is
dropped.

We also use specialized arithmetic to compute the quadratic form
using matrix division that's specialized for a triangular matrix,
where this gets called in a loop for each y in the sequence
of variates (may just be one if the argument isn't an array of
vectors):

  sum_lp_vec += dot_self(mdivide_left_tri_low(L, y_minus_mu));

and then the whole result gets multiplied at once and subtracted
from the accumulator:

  lp -= 0.5 * sum_lp_vec;

Eigen's great!

- Bob

> On Jan 13, 2017, at 4:44 AM, Conner DiPaolo <cdip...@g.hmc.edu> wrote:
>
> Turns out you were correct in saying that working directly on the log-scale can make the arithmetic more robust. Specifically, the Cholesky parametrized normal likelihood was the issue, and using the following representation directly (dropping the 2pi constant) lets the model run (even with opt, haven't tried out vb yet though will report back when I do). I wonder if this was a problem with using the Sigma = LL' factorization when L didn't have positive diagonal entries, and therefore wasn't the _Cholesky_ factorization, even though the math could be the same. If Stan assumes that the diagonal elements are positive, the log determinant could be computed more efficiently (see below: the square in L_ii^2 could be brought out of the sum as a scaling factor). In that case, taking the log of L_ii could be undefined (in the real plane) and return infinity or something. Does Stan do this under the hood?
>

> <image.png>

>
> On Thu, Jan 5, 2017 at 6:03 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> I don't see any error message there.  Are you using the latest
> PyStan?  This may just mean that some of the arithmetic underflows

> You can print out target() as you go:

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] STAN Posterior sampling question
messages.body_plain:
This kind of model is referred to as a “intractable likelihood” model in
the statistics literature and it cannot be done in Stan.  The problem is
computing that normalizing term — the only way to we know how to
compute high-dimensional intervals accurately is MCMC!  There are
Sequential Monte Carlo approaches that formally give an answer,
but they can be difficult to scale to the scope of these problems.

Ultimately this is a screaming application of the “Folk Theorem”.
You probably don’t want to built this model but rather another model
that doesn’t integrate out the marginalized parameters at all and instead
tries to fit everything jointly.

> On Jan 14, 2017, at 8:06 AM, Samuel Hinton <samue...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> As to what I am unable to put into stan, it is a high dimensional integral that appears on the denominator of the likelihood, not the numerator, so the standard way of marginalising over parameters doesn't won't work. If there is a way to put a theta-dependent integral on the denominator of the joint lpdf I would be very happy to break free of my ignorance!

This documentation issue might also be present in other Cholesky parameterized densities, though I haven't checked.

> > Apparently, it's what physicists have been doing for years.  There

> >
> > If N is the number of trials and theta the simplex of distributions

> >
> >   X ~ Multinomial(N, theta)
> >
> > then
> >
> >   E[X[n]] = N * theta[n]
> >
> > and we can approximate
> >
> >   Multinomial(X | N, theta)
> >
> >   ~approx~
> >
> >   PROD_k Poisson(X[k] | N * theta[k])
> >
> > In vectorized Stan notation, that'd just be

> Since this assumes that L_{ii} > 0 for all i, I'd suggest revising the relevant section 57.3 for the multi_normal_cholesky to make this explicit because it currently says that the parameterization is valid if L is lower triangular and Sigma = L L^T, which includes L_{ii} potentially non-positive. I can submit a pull request tomorrow as this is probably really simple to change unless there's some other protocol to changing documentation. This documentation issue might also be present in other Cholesky parameterized densities, though I haven't checked.
>
> On Sat, Jan 14, 2017 at 6:28 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Yes, the determinant calculation for the Cholesky-parameterized
> multi-normal is done efficiently.  Ben keeps a close watch on
> our linear algebra for critical functions like this.
>
> The relevant code for the determinant is in
>
>   stan/math/prim/mat/prob/multi_normal_cholesky_lpdf.hpp
>
> and looks just like you'd expect for Cholesky factor L and
> log density accumulator lp (recall the determinant is in
> the denominator of the density).
>
>         lp -= L.diagonal().array().log().sum() * size_vec;
>
> size_vec is the number of variates, so that we only compute
> this determinant once if it's called with an array of
> variates.  That is, if we call y ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L) and y
> is an array of vectors.  Then rather than computing it and adding
> it for each vector element of y, we just multiply.
>
> Also, we use template traits programming to wrap this in a static
> conditional that only includes the decrement if the matrix L
> isn't data.  If it's data, the result is a constant term and is
> dropped.
>
> We also use specialized arithmetic to compute the quadratic form
> using matrix division that's specialized for a triangular matrix,
> where this gets called in a loop for each y in the sequence
> of variates (may just be one if the argument isn't an array of
> vectors):
>
>   sum_lp_vec += dot_self(mdivide_left_tri_low(L, y_minus_mu));
>
> and then the whole result gets multiplied at once and subtracted
> from the accumulator:
>
>   lp -= 0.5 * sum_lp_vec;
>
> Eigen's great!
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Is there a function in Stan analogous to the convolve() function in R?
messages.subject_clean: Is there a function in Stan analogous to the convolve() function in R?
messages.body_plain:
Dear User Group,

I am trying to fit a model in Stan that views a particular time-series as arising from the convolution of several “pulses” of varying strength along with a particular response function. As a starting point, I am interested in recreating the analysis reported here by another research tea, (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3365158/) with original scripts in R provided here (http://www.pnas.org/content/suppl/2012/05/11/1201858109.DCSupplemental/sd02.txt and http://www.pnas.org/content/suppl/2012/05/11/1201858109.DCSupplemental/sd03.txt). I have an intuition as to how I should proceed, but a critical step in the original R calculations involves the command:

convolve(i,rev(h),type="open")

Where i represents the pulses and h represents the response function. Does Stan have an equivalent command to convolve(x, y, type='open')? I have been unable to find one.

Cheers!
Jon

On Sunday, January 15, 2017 at 9:02:22 PM UTC-5, Heather wrote:
> I am relatively new to stan and even newer to rstanarm so my apologies for this basic question.  I am trying to build a three level model where I pool slopes at both levels but not intercepts. In stan_lmer, I haven't been able to figure out how to specify priors for the global slope. Specifically, I'd like to use sigma as my scale parameter, so maybe something like- prior=normal(0, scale=sigma)? In stan, I would have it written as: b_thirdlevel~normal(mu_b, sigma_b).

That is not possible in rstanarm; the arguments to the function passed to the prior argument have to be constants. It might be possible in brms.

But if by sigma you mean the standard deviation of the errors in a Gaussian model, that is a weird prior belief because as sigma approaches 0, beta approaches 0, which would only work if the outcome was a constant. In Gaussian models, the normal prior on the b terms is already being scaled by sigma.

Ben

messages.subject: Stan (MCMC) with vague prior gives different results compared to MLE or "bayesglm" ?
messages.subject_clean: Stan (MCMC) with vague prior gives different results compared to MLE or "bayesglm" ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan experts,

I am trying to implement a GLM model (binomial likelihood) with logit link using Stan when there is so-called "sparse data bias" as defined by Greenland et al. (2016) (http://www.bmj.com/content/352/bmj.i1981) or seperation problems as discussed in Gelman et al. (2008)(http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/priors11.pdf).

Dataset is coming from randomized controlled trial and as follows (the original source is: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9920948):

# dataset
# responders sampleSize treatment
# 1               30               control
# 23              59               experimental

The observed odds ratio is 23 * 29  / 36 = 18.5, so log OD: 2.92.

Firstly, I fitted the model using MLE (via glm function), I get the estimate 2.92 and standard deviation 1.05.

Secondly, I used "bayesglm" function from "arm" package with normal prior with mean zero and variance 10000, then the estimate is 2.91 (stdev 1.05).

Thirdly, I used "stan_glm" function from "rstanarm" package with normal prior with mean zero and variance 10000, BUT then the posterior mean estimate is 3.54 (stdev 1.37). As you notice it is substantially different from previous values. It can't be "rstanarm" issue, since I have tried using directly Stan which gives same result. Also I tried JAGS which again gave very close result to 3.54 (stdev 1.37)). So maybe it is a MCMC issue.

This is strange for me. I know that I need to use "penalization" for MLE or "weakly informative prior" such as cauchy(0, 2.5), but this is not issue in this case. Somehow MCMC overestimates more in this specific dataset compares to MLE. When I use the Firth correction, estimates are 2.54 (with stdev 0.9) or when I use bayesglm with cauchy(0, 2.5) then the result is 2.55 (stdev 0.86). BUT when I use Stan with cauchy(0, 2.5), then the estimate is 2.93 (stdev. 1.1). Hence, MCMC still overestimates the treatment effect.

My question is "am I missing something trivial?" OR "what would be the possible explanation so that MCMC results differ from "arm" and MLE results?

I attached the R code which produce these results.

Thank you very much for your help,

Burak

The arm::bayesglm function is essentially returning a posterior mode; the rstanarm::stan_glm function is returning a posterior median or you could calculate the posterior mean, both of which are preferable to a mode. If the posterior is skewed, you could get results like this.

Ben

Yes. But it is more specific than "MCMC with flat priors". It is tautological to say that the posterior mean or median will differ from the mode of the likelihood function when the posterior distribution is skewed. I would also expect the posterior to often be skewed in applications like this.

> And, normally I think I should trust MCMC results more than MLE results, but in this application, don't you think that MCMC causes more biased results compared to MLE? because MCMC give median estimate for odds ratio 26 , while MLE gives 18 and Firth correction gives 12? SO MCMC more overestimate the treatment effect?

If the posterior distribution is skewed, then the asymptotic assumptions of MLEs are not holding because both the posterior distribution and the sampling distribution are multivariate normal under the same asymptotic conditions.

In hierarchical models and mixture models, you often don't even have an MLE.
Or it may degenerate to a boundary.  In many of these cases, the posterior
mean will be well defined.

As Ben says, if the posterior is skewed, the mode won't equal the mean.
The posterior mean is the point estimate minimizing expected squared error
vs. the true estimate;  the posterior median minimizes expected absolute
error.  The posterior mode has no interpretation and depends on parameterization.

If you're doing MLE, you can think of the prior as a penalty term.  Or
you can think in terms of calculating the posterior mode of the Bayesian
model (which doesn't really have an interpretation as it depends on
the parameterization, unlike the posterior mean).

This might help:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html

> Just for my own edification, why aren't the .cpp files generated in a configure script instead? Isn't configure called by build and install?

The configure{.win} script is called by build but not install (unless you pass --preclean). Also, the Build and Reload button in RStudio passes --preclean, which is not always what you want (it recompiles the C++ even if you have only changed the R), so we came up with an ingenious hack to pass an invalid option called --precleanOOPS that prevents this. Check out the rstanarm.Rproj file on GitHub.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
After more experimentation I came to the conclusion that this approach (marginalization over multiple imputeted ordered variables) is to slow for my data set.

An alternative approach that seems to work is to rescale the original data to lie between 0 and 1, apply a logit transform to the rescaled data, and to impute data using a multivariate normal distribution (for the rescaled and logit-transformed data). This approach is reasonably faithful to the (my) data and orders of magnitude faster than the original approach.

messages.subject: Issues with a Stan-based R package
messages.subject_clean: Issues with a Stan-based R package
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan Developers,

My colleagues and I made a Stan-based R packaged called hBayesDM (GitHub: https://github.com/CCS-Lab, tutorial: rpubs.com/CCSL/hBayesDM <http://rpubs.com/CCSL/hBayesDM>). Thanks to feedback form StanCon reviewers, I tried to include precompiled Stan models and follow some of the guidelines for Stan-based R packages (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstantools/vignettes/developer-guidelines.html).

Now the latest version (0.3.0) has precompiled models, which run much faster now (thanks!). But there are a few things I could not fix or understand, which are listed below. I think they are related to some C coding or parallel sampling, but I'm not sure.

1. If I use multiple cores for parallel sampling in RStudio or base R Console, I get the following messages. But if I run the same code in a Mac terminal, I don't have any issues. If I don't use parallel sampling (set 'ncore' to 1), then everything is fine even in RStudio or base R Console. It's very strange to me.

I opened an issue about this in the hBayesDM GitHub repository and you can see the summary here: https://github.com/CCS-Lab/hBayesDM/issues/11

2. There is an error during installation. Please see the following sentences highlighted in red:

check("hBayesDM", cran = T)

* R * exec * inst * preparing package for lazy loading * help ** installing help indices * building package indices * testing if installed package can be loaded Error in .doLoadActions(where, attach) : error in load action .__A__.1 for package hBayesDM: is(module, "character"): object 'm' not found Error: loading failed Execution halted ERROR: loading failed
removing ‘/private/var/folders/jb/3202zzgd5j304l5pb6yv4_6w0000gn/T/RtmpqAC81F/hBayesDM.Rcheck/hBayesDM’

This error might be critical? error in load action .__A__.1 for package hBayesDM: is(module, "character"): object 'm' not found

Even with the error above, I can install the package: by installing the package directly from GitHub or using the command like 'R CMD INSTALL hBayesDM'.

3. To include precompiled models, I used the Ben Goodrich's suggestion in this post (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/iBjP4Qq7aP4). Now each model's *.rds file is in the '/exec' folder along with *.stan files. I'm not sure if this is the best practice for including precompiled models. Any suggestions/recommendations would be highly appreciated.

These are some of the posts I found from the Stan mailing list.

1. https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/GlobalEnv$20core%7Csort:relevance/stan-users/tyD6maC7RRg/cWUNHzIGBQAJ

2. https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/GlobalEnv%7Csort:relevance/stan-users/P-kZHokKg3c/I6ZHHP5mAAAJ

3. https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/JlYv7Rt6-zM

I know there are several things that need to be improved in the package and it would be great if Stan developers can help. Thanks a lot for your help in advance and please let me know if you have any questions.

Best,
Young Ahn

Linas

> After more experimentation I came to the conclusion that this approach (marginalization over multiple imputeted ordered variables) is to slow for my data set.
>
> An alternative approach that seems to work is to rescale the original data to lie between 0 and 1, apply a logit transform to the rescaled data, and to impute data using a multivariate normal distribution (for the rescaled and logit-transformed data). This approach is reasonably faithful to the (my) data and orders of magnitude faster than the original approach.

> On Wednesday, December 14, 2016 at 9:46:32 PM UTC+1, Guido Biele wrote:
> just to make sure that I understand what your are saying:
>
> lets say we have a design matrix for a regression model x_imputed, which consists mostly of observed data, but some entries of which are parameters (i.e. imputed).
> If we now focus on one row of x and want multiplicate x_imputed[n,] with regressions weights beta, are you saying that then it would be fastest to do straight forward matrix multiplication for the rows that consist only of data, and to separate data from parameters in a rows of x_imputed that contains parameters before multiplying each predictor with its weight beta?

> guido

> On Wed, Dec 14, 2016 at 5:20 PM Daniel Lee   wrote:
> Hi Guido,
>

> Given my limited math and programming background,
> its probably wise I stick to the "follow best paractice" option.
>
> [about what eta, x and b are: eta and b are parameters, and
> x is a mix of parameters (used to imputed missing data) and
> data.]
>
> If that's what it is, the fastest you can do it is to split x into the parameters and the data and do those operations separately. Then you lose the generality of jamming everything into one vector, but that's really going to be faster.
>
> I wouldn't suggest it in general, though. It makes it complicated and hard to code. There's a tradeoff between fast computation and fast / robust coding. I'd rather code things that are slower than I'm less likely to make a mistake than to code something super fast and wrong.
>
>
>
> Daniel

> Figure 1 in the paper shows an expression graph.
> Is it correct to say that if I have column and row
> vectors x and b of length 3, then if I write anywhere

> and an expression tree with 3 levels, whereas
> eta = x * b;
> results in only 3 automatic differentiation variables
> and an expression tree of 2 levels?
>

>
> There's a large section in the paper about how we actually implement the C++ so that we cut out lots of the expression graph. So... no, you're not right here.
>
> If you were to write the expressions in C++ directly without using built in functions, then yes, you're right. (in the second expression, eta = x * b, you'd have to write eta = stan::math::multiply(x, b), but yes).
>
>
>
> Daniel
>
>
> Guido
>
>

>

One of the parameters there is h_std, which is a vector of size T, the number of trading days. Thus, being in the parameters block it is included in the NUTS resampling procedure. This appears to slow the process down. Stan users guide in section 5.6 states:
"There is a substantial amount of computation involved for parameter variables in a Stan program at each leapfrog step within the HMC or NUTS samplers, and a bit more computation along with writes involved for saving the parameter values corresponding to a sample."

It makes sense. However in this case the most meaningful parameters are those three: mu, phi and sigma. I don't really care about the distribution of h_std every trading day. In addition to speed concerns, I'm also concerned that Stan would concentrate on getting all those h_std right and not on other important parameters.

Would it make sense to let only mu, phi and sigma to be the only model parameters and let h_std being regenerated every time a new sample is drawn? It doesn't seem to be possible though, since _rng functions are not allowed in either model or transformed parameters.

Thanks!

messages.subject: Coverage - beta expectation
messages.subject_clean: Coverage - beta expectation
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Best wishes first to your incredible team !

Some months ago, I came up with having different results <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/5Y5_HWZ0SCY/46toOmSJCgAJ> when using different parametrizations of the same model (mainly, in term of sd and in term of precision = 1/sd^2). I realised at this time that intervals obtained with the "sd" parametrization were extremely large when degrees of freedom (df) were low, for both the parameters and the predictions (beta-expectation tolerance intervals). When I said "large" at this time, I already meant "larger than what is expected because of low df".

At the time, we had some discussion on priors, on Jacobians, on some additional good advice for model implementation, etc., and the last point not yet discussed was to check carefully the coverage; namely, to see if the obtained prediction intervals were of expectation beta (if beta is the expected coverage).

So, I did the simulations. Here, with a simple linear regression (assume it is a model for a variable recorded along the time). I'll look at the coverage for the prediction of a single time point. I fixed beta at 95% (because as a statistician, I cannot come with a better idea :-D ), and I looked at the expected/average coverage across all simulations.

Four files are attached, all self running (data are generated each time):
- Frequentist classical prediction interval (i.e. the beta-expectation tolerance interval, in this case)
- MCMCregress (package MCMCpack) implementation of the same.
- Stan implementation of the same with uniform prior (I also try with other implementations, e.g. centred X, as done with brms package.), and inv_gamma [message edited to add it]. Might be better with inv_gamma prior for support, but uniform shouldn't lead to that much trouble.

For Bayesian framework, again, I tried to be non informative with Stan, i.e. using improper uniform prior. Indeed, in a simulation exercise, I don't want to / cannot use as prior what I know from my simulated data. Similar for inv_gamma prior. For MCMCregress, I did not specify any prior (I let the default, which is similar to one would assumed non-informative with conjugate prior, i.e. inverse_gamma(0.0001,0.0001) for sigma^2).

Results are all good for both the Frequentist estimates and Bayesian MCMCregress results (on plots, blue line must be on top of the red line, located at beta=95% coverage). However, Stan coverages with uniform priors are over-estimated when df are low (i.e. blue line higher than red line in small df cases, i.e. not of beta-expectation). This is really embarrassing as small data remains the common place in many domains. From previous experiments, all other Gibbs or M-H based samplers perform better with low df (but really I like Stan language and flexibilities so much... :-) ). Stan is "stabilized" with inv_gamma prior, but coverage are always "just a little bit too low". I would have preferred the opposite :-s.

I did not check precisely, but I am sure that the posterior distribution of the parameters does not exhibit good coverage properties in the uniform case (the predictive only borrows their own variabilities). It would mean the exploration of the posterior distribution with NUTS has some trouble here.

Fortunately, most user of samplers tend to be careful with the use of their results. But this type of issue seems more difficult to handle and detect, in my opinion (in my case, on the previous posts (see link above), intervals were so large that I did not believe in them, and I had Frequentist approximations to figure it out, but in some cases... well... it might be dangerous).
Fortunately, again, these results are conservative (intervals too large), which in most of the time protect the statistician, but not always as with the inverse gamma.

Any idea of what would cause that and if there is a way, or a plan, to improve/correct that ?

Also, keep up with the awesome work up to there.

Kind regards,
-----------
Pierre

ps: try to run the code with Stan twice in a row. On my machine, R crashes completely the second time, at the time of model compilation... That's probably a problem with parallelism, but the way it is done (Stan not in parallel, simulations in parallel) is the fastest I've found.

messages.subject: Print Slow, Even with Excluded Variables
messages.subject_clean: Print Slow, Even with Excluded Variables
messages.body_plain:
Print has an option to set include=FALSE, which means that the character vector passed to pars excludes the listed variables. I have some variables that are very large, so excluding them is natural. However, print is very slow, even with these large variables excluded.

I found it interesting that when I then run print a second time, removing one of the excluded variables (i.e., including it in the print operation), the call to print is essentially instantaneous. This suggests to me that all the results of print are calculated for all the variables upon it's first time being called. These results are then cached for any future call.

If this is a correct understanding of how it works, I suggest that the print command should only do the calculations necessary to print the results (it can still cache them for future use).

messages.body_plain:
Hi John, this actually has to do with the summary method (called internally by print). Check out the use_cache argument to the summary method for stanfit objects (help(`summary,stanfit-method`)). Essentially, what's going on is that, by default, the first time you run summary (even if indirectly by calling print), if the use_cache argument is set to TRUE then it will compute the summary statistics for all parameters and generated quantities and then cache them so that all future times you call summary or print the output can be taken from the cached summaries instead of computed every time. This is a bit strange, but it's particularly useful for models with lots of parameters because instead of print and summary being slow every time, they are only slow the first time. To disable this you can set use_cache=FALSE when calling summary or when calling print (because print passes arguments to summary via ...).

Hope that helps,

Jonah

After having read your messages several times and the part of Stan manual which explains MLE and Bayesian mode estimation etc., I think I understand the point.
