messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] goodness of fit of PK hierarchical stan models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] goodness of fit of PK hierarchical stan models
messages.body_plain:
Linus,

traditional goodness-of-fit diagnostics in PK-realm don't necessarily translate well to PBPK, as the model simplifications implicit with compartmental models allow for more reasonable mapping of parameters to data. Eg, given a one compartment model with CL/V and concentration data, doing a visual or posterior predictive check can help easily identify where model misspecification arises, and the parameter the maps to that portion of the data (eg. trough concentrations missed = problems with CL or compartmental structure)

Likewise CWRES-vs-IDV type plots and DV vs IPRED diagnostics are also similarly used, but don't map well to the multitude of PBPK params.

My advice is, as with simpler models, identify the key questions the model is trying to address, and most importantly use quality science and mechanistic knowledge to drive the model construction. Then supplement with diagnostic plots that adequately show that such a model is not unduly biased to address those questions. For example, given a therapeutic window of 10 ng/mL efficacy cutpoint, given a PPC that shows that at the 10th 50th and 90th percentiles, the observed and fit data are aligned, gives confidence that your model can suitably address the question at hand, even if, say, the peak concentrations are slightly off.

Sensitivity analysis of the param values, and leveraging prior literature to inform your priors, and some basic diagnostics similar to those mentioned above should be sufficient I would think.

Here are some helpful links

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2751255/
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4761232/

>           (1. - 3. /(2.*y)) * PIG(y-1,mu,tau) +
>            mu^2 / (1+2.*tau*mu) / (y*(y-1)) * PIG(y-2,mu,tau);

------ Original Message ------

> Linus,
>
> traditional goodness-of-fit diagnostics in PK-realm don't necessarily translate well to PBPK, as the model simplifications implicit with compartmental models allow for more reasonable mapping of parameters to data. Eg, given a one compartment model with CL/V and concentration data, doing a visual or posterior predictive check can help easily identify where model misspecification arises, and the parameter the maps to that portion of the data (eg. trough concentrations missed = problems with CL or compartmental structure)
>
> Likewise CWRES-vs-IDV type plots and DV vs IPRED diagnostics are also similarly used, but don't map well to the multitude of PBPK params.
>
> My advice is, as with simpler models, identify the key questions the model is trying to address, and most importantly use quality science and mechanistic knowledge to drive the model construction. Then supplement with diagnostic plots that adequately show that such a model is not unduly biased to address those questions. For example, given a therapeutic window of 10 ng/mL efficacy cutpoint, given a PPC that shows that at the 10th 50th and 90th percentiles, the observed and fit data are aligned, gives confidence that your model can suitably address the question at hand, even if, say, the peak concentrations are slightly off.
>
> Sensitivity analysis of the param values, and leveraging prior literature to inform your priors, and some basic diagnostics similar to those mentioned above should be sufficient I would think.
>
> Here are some helpful links
>
> https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2751255/
> https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4761232/

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Mixture model problem
messages.body_plain:
Just curious. I have a quick question about mixtures, and thought I'd piggy back off this, since it's a simple example.

If you wanted to allow individuals differing probabilities of 'belonging' to one component or another, would you estimate per-individual probabilities with a hierarchical prior? I've done this, but I never see others do it, so I'm worried I'm in the wrong.

That is, instead of simplex[K] lambda, could you have:
simplex[K] lambda[N]; // N = number of individuals
for(n in 1:N){
lambda[n] ~ dirichlet(params here);
}

or, in the simpler case of K=2:
vector[N] lambda_logit;
vector[N] lambda_logit_mu;
lambda_logit_mu = some + latent + class + predictors;
lambda_logit ~ logistic(lambda_logit_mu, 1); //And how do you choose the error to this? 1? 3? estimate it?

Mainly, I'm just curious, because when specifying mixtures in, e.g., gibbs using a non-marginalized approach, each individual's membership may be ~ categorical(.2,.3,.5), but p(k_i = 1 | ...) = .8 (not .2).
Yet when using a marginalized model, you aren't estimating p(k_i = 1|D), but the parameters to the categorical prior (so to speak); so how can you obtain p(k_i = 1 | D) from a model that only estimates the prior?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture of gamma distributions from interval data
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Mixture of gamma distributions from interval data
messages.body_plain:
Do you get lots of warning messages about divergences?
If you're not seeing output in RStan, try running in one
chain.  I don't know about the other interfaces but
CmdStan just pipes out warnings directly, whereas RStan
buffers them.

You might want to put tighter priors with less heavy tails
on dist_shape and dist_rate.  The CDFs get very flat in the
tails.

For speed, you should compute

  vector[K] log_theta = log(theta);

and reuse it rather than repeating the computation N times.

I'd normally suggest working on a log scale, but I don't know
if that'll help here given our poor log cdf implementations.

  real pp = log_diff_exp(gamma_lcdf(...), gamma_lcdf(...));

At the very least, it should avoid the possible catastrophic
cancellations you get with the direct difference.

The other way you can code this model is with the latent x.
But for that, each x needs a different lower and upper bound,
which means writing your own Jacobians until we can generalize
the lower and upper bound syntax in Stan (on our to-do list).

- Bob

> On Jan 31, 2017, at 9:41 AM, Ron <rcdr...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I'm trying to estimate the parameters of two Gamma distributions from data assumed to come from a mixture of them.
>
> I took the mixture of two Normal distributions example from the Stan reference and modified to use Gamma distributions and to account for my observations being an interval rather than a point, that is each x value is observed to lie between x_lower and x_upper.
>
> data {
>   int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
>   int<lower=1> N; // number of data points
>   real x_lower[N]; // interval observations: lower
>   real x_upper[N]; //                        & upper
> }
> parameters {
>   simplex[K] theta; // mixing proportions
>   real<lower=0> dist_shape[K]; // shape |- of each gamma dist
>   real<lower=0> dist_rate[K];  // rate  |
> }
> model {
>   dist_shape ~ cauchy(0, 10);
>   dist_rate ~ cauchy(0, 1);
>   for (n in 1:N) {
>     real ps[K]; // temp for log component densities
>     real pp;
>     for (k in 1:K) {
>       pp = gamma_cdf( x_upper[n], dist_shape[k], dist_rate[k] ) -
>             gamma_cdf( x_lower[n], dist_shape[k], dist_rate[k] );
>       ps[k] = log(theta[k]) + log(pp);
>     }
>     target += log_sum_exp(ps);
>   }
> }
>

>
> I've tried it with the actual data we want to analyse and some simulated data that should be clearer (as well as having known outputs), but it doesn't appear to be working.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Mixture model problem
messages.body_plain:
You aren't getting the kind of data you need to fit
that simplex, even hierarchically.  You only get
one observation and you have (K-1) free parameters.
And it's not like you have overdispersion or something
to fit---you still are just selecting a single group
for membership.

What people often do is have some predictors that
effect membership and instead of a simplex, they
build a multi-logit regression (or a logit if there
are only two categories).  For example, in the movement
HMM models in ecology, the probability of an animal
being in a state can depend on time of day, distance
to water, previous movements, etc.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture model problem
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Mixture model problem
messages.body_plain:
Ok, so lets assume you have K=2 latent groups, and you're parameterizing via logits (which is what I tend to do).

If you don't have latent group predictors, and you want to fit a mixture (in essence, an intercept-only model), then the manual's method is the way you'd go; you don't estimate pi_logit[n] for each person, but pi_logit as a prior; then you convert to pi, then use that to compute a posterior probability of group membership?
E.g., for(n in 1:N){ target += log_mix(pi, lpdf(y[n] | params[1]), lpdf(y[n] | params[2]) }; then later, you compute simplex[2] pi_n[N] manually, by solving for p(k=2 | y_i)?

If you *do* have latent group predictors, and you want to fit a mixture, then you CAN estimate pi_logit[n] for each person, and put the converted pi straight into the likelihood?
E.g., for(n in 1:N){ target += log_mix(pi[n], lpdf(y[n] | params[1]), lpdf(y[n] | params[2]) }; where logit(pi[n]) = some + latent + group + predictors; then you manually compute p(k = 2 | y_i) as above?

I... think I have some work to do on my model. This may actually solve a major identifiability issue in my model.

TLDR; I was conceptually fitting a per-person likelihood that is: pi[n]*f(y[n] | params[1]) + (1 - pi[n])*f(y[n] | params[2]); logit(pi[n]) ~ logistic(pi_predicted[n], 1), and using pi[n] as posterior membership probability, and pi_predicted[n] as either the overall "prior" membership logit (if intercept-only model) or predicted membership probability.

Instead of: pi*f(y[n] | params[1]) + (1 - pi)*f(y[n] | params[2]); then manually computing posterior membership probability by solving for p(k = 2 | y_i) = p(y_i | k = 2)p(k = 2) / (sum_k^2(p(y_i | k)p(k))
I think I can use this ^^, and still predict pi[n] (using logit modeling), but it will need to be deterministic (no ~ logistic(pi_predicted[n]); instead you fit the model and still manually compute the posterior membership prob.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture model problem
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Mixture model problem
messages.body_plain:
> On Jan 31, 2017, at 2:03 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Ok, so lets assume you have K=2 latent groups, and you're parameterizing via logits (which is what I tend to do).
>
> If you don't have latent group predictors, and you want to fit a mixture (in essence, an intercept-only model), then the manual's method is the way you'd go; you don't estimate pi_logit[n] for each person, but pi_logit as a prior; then you convert to pi, then use that to compute a posterior probability of group membership?

> E.g., for(n in 1:N){ target += log_mix(pi, lpdf(y[n] | params[1]), lpdf(y[n] | params[2]) }; then later, you compute simplex[2] pi_n[N] manually, by solving for p(k=2 | y_i)?

Yes, see below.

> If you *do* have latent group predictors, and you want to fit a mixture, then you CAN estimate pi_logit[n] for each person, and put the converted pi straight into the likelihood?
> E.g., for(n in 1:N){ target += log_mix(pi[n], lpdf(y[n] | params[1]), lpdf(y[n] | params[2]) }; where logit(pi[n]) = some + latent + group + predictors; then you manually compute p(k = 2 | y_i) as above?

Exactly.

> I... think I have some work to do on my model. This may actually solve a major identifiability issue in my model.
>
> TLDR; I was conceptually fitting a per-person likelihood that is: pi[n]*f(y[n] | params[1]) + (1 - pi[n])*f(y[n] | params[2]); logit(pi[n]) ~ logistic(pi_predicted[n], 1), and using pi[n] as posterior membership probability, and pi_predicted[n] as either the overall "prior" membership logit (if intercept-only model) or predicted membership probability.
>
> Instead of: pi*f(y[n] | params[1]) + (1 - pi)*f(y[n] | params[2]); then manually computing posterior membership probability by solving for p(k = 2 | y_i) = p(y_i | k = 2)p(k = 2) / (sum_k^2(p(y_i | k)p(k))
> I think I can use this ^^, and still predict pi[n] (using logit modeling), but it will need to be deterministic (no ~ logistic(pi_predicted[n]); instead you fit the model and still manually compute the posterior membership prob.

If we let the density for each mixture component be

  ps[1, n] = pi * f(y[n] | params[1])

  ps[2, n] = (1 - pi) * f(y[n] | params[2])

then we have

  Pr[z[n] = 1] = ps[1, n] / (ps[1, n] + ps[2, n])

or more stably,

  log Pr[z[n] = 1] = log ps[1, n] - log_sum_exp(ps[1, n], ps[2, n]))

where, e.g.,

  log ps[1, n] = log(pi) + log(f(y[n] | params[1]))

- Bob

exploit to simplify computations.  If you make a data-dependent
prior, you lose the nice asymptotic guarantees of Bayesian
inference because you don't have a fixed prior.

Hi Scott,

I think there's some misunderstanding.

If you've followed the instructions and have installed the C++ toolchain that we suggested (RTools), then you're ready to go from Stan programs to machine executable code.

You'll need to supply a Stan program to make it work, though. That's why I tried to point you to the example-models repo. Stan is a language, so you can write whatever model you're interested in. It's not like other toolkits where you build it and toss data at it.

If you have specific questions about how to get started or if you're still confused, please let us know where in the directions you're lost.

Daniel
